claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be synthesized with systematically different pre-existing defect densities.
Rapid quenching produces a higher defect density than slower cooling or post-synthesis annealing.
Grain boundaries, dislocation networks, and vacancy clusters are localized high-energy sites in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Pre-existing structural defects lower the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement associated with melting.
The reduced local rearrangement barrier decreases the premelting-onset temperature.
Premelting initiates preferentially at identifiable structural defects.
Liquid formed locally at defect sites propagates gradually through the nanoparticle.
High-defect FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will exhibit premelting at a lower temperature than low-defect nanoparticles.
High-defect nanoparticles will undergo a more gradual and spatially heterogeneous phase transition.
Defect-reduced nanoparticles will have a higher and sharper melting onset.
An abrupt melting transition is characteristic of a homogeneous, low-defect solid nanoparticle.
Two composition-matched batches should be compared under the same 600–1400 °C inert-atmosphere thermal ramp.
In situ TEM and high-energy X-ray diffraction can be used to compare melting onset, spatial initiation, and phase evolution between the batches.
The proposed defect-controlled behavior is limited to the tested nanoparticle-size regime and inert atmosphere.
Changes in nanoparticle size or exposure to reactive gases may alter the thermal-transition behavior.
Variability in defect distributions and minor compositional segregation may change the quantitative premelting-onset difference.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant decrease in premelting onset or a more gradual transition in the high-defect batch would falsify the hypothesis.
